title: Machig Labdrön
hook: the Tibetan woman teacher who, tradition says, founded chöd, offering the body to fear

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gampopa, the doctor who became a monk. Your line: two streams.

A burial ground at night, high on the Tibetan plateau. Wind, a scatter of bones, a small hand drum in one hand and a bell in the other. Someone sits down in the one place everyone else walks around, and does it on purpose. Tradition traces this practice to a woman named Machig Labdrön, a reader of the Perfection of Wisdom sutras who became a teacher with students of her own. What she taught sounds backward at first: walk toward the thing that frightens you, and offer it a meal.
screen: `A BURIAL GROUND AT NIGHT.` → `A DRUM AND A BELL.` → `WALK TOWARD THE FEAR.`

segments.voice: First, the name of her practice: chöd, a Tibetan word meaning to cut. What gets cut is not a person, and not really a demon. In her teaching, the true demon is the grip of the self, the habit of clutching at me and mine, and fear is where that grip shows itself most plainly. Second, the method. In the visualization, the practitioner imagines leaving the body behind and offering it as food and nectar to every hungry being, the gentle guests and the frightening ones alike. Nothing is held back. The point is not to act brave. It is to stop guarding the very thing fear is trying to protect. Third, the root. Machig's practice rests on the Perfection of Wisdom sutras, which teach that nothing has a separate, solid self. Chöd takes that teaching off the page and into the dark: if there is no solid self, whatever the demon eats was never really owned. Fourth, a woman's lineage. Her life stories describe a teacher who had a family, raised children, and gathered students, and tradition says her teaching even traveled from Tibet back to India, a stream flowing the other way. Chöd is still practiced in Tibetan Buddhism, often with the drum and bell, and it is traditionally received from a teacher after preparation. It is not a dare. It is generosity, aimed at the thing you'd rather run from.
screen: `CHÖD: CUTTING THE GRIP OF SELF.` · `OFFER THE BODY TO EVERY HUNGRY BEING.` · `THE PERFECTION OF WISDOM, IN THE DARK.` · `A WOMAN'S LINEAGE.` · then, large: `GENEROSITY AIMED AT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small fear, not the biggest one, a phone call you keep putting off or a worry about a bill, and notice where it shows up in the body. Don't push it away, and don't feed the story; turn toward it the way you'd turn toward a guest at the door, letting your hands open a little on each out-breath. If it grows too big, come back to the breath alone.
Machig Labdrön. The Tibetan teacher whom tradition credits with chöd, cutting the grip of self by offering it to fear. Today's word.
Your line: offer it to fear. Whatever it eats was never really yours to guard. Day nine hundred seventy-seven, done.

howItsDone: Chöd is practiced in Tibetan Buddhist communities, usually after receiving it from a teacher, with chanted liturgy, a hand drum and bell, and a visualized offering of the body; some practitioners do it in lonely or frightening places.

chat.says: Why would anyone sit in a burial ground at night on purpose? Is chöd about being brave?
options: No, it's generosity: offering even the self, to cut the grip that fear guards.
Yes, it's a test of nerve: whoever stays all night proves they're fearless.
It's to scare yourself so often that you stop feeling anything at all.
chat.meaning: Chöd means to cut. The practitioner offers the body to every hungry being, cutting the grip of self. It is generosity, not a dare.
